body_markdown:
In 2008, Ron Fogarty, now 76, of Brownstown, Michigan, retired from his career as a certified electrician. With time on his hands, he decided to create the car of his dreams.


“I found a ’49 Chevy business coupe on Facebook Marketplace which I snapped up for $1300,” Fogarty explains. “Except for a bit of rust in the rocker panels, it was in perfect condition. My goal was to own a car older than me which I could build into what resembled a drag racer competing in the[Gas Class of the 1950s and ‘60s](https://www.hagerty.com/media/motorsports/gallery-vintage-drag-racing-invades-ohios-dragway-42/) .”


“I had two partners in this crime. A close friend, John Martin, started with a 454 Chevy big-block V-8 for power, to which he fitted aluminum heads, a hydraulic flat-tappet camshaft from Comp Cams, roller rocker arms, MSD electronic ignition, and a dual-feed Holley 750 four-barrel carb. There’s been no dyno test, but a conservative guess is over 500 horses under my hood.


Fogarty’s son-in-law Mike Hale provided the aforementioned aluminum heads plus a Hydramatic TH400 three-speed automatic transmission, and they added a shift kit. “The B&M shifter we fitted is clumsy to operate but visually perfect for this application,” says Fogarty. Mike also provided a rear axle from a Chevy ZR2 S10 pickup equipped with disc brakes and a 3.73:1 final-drive ratio.


Courtesy Ron Fogarty


“Mike is an accomplished fabricator, so he made the modifications to the Chevy frame needed to accommodate the rear axle, which is secured by twin ladder bars and a short Panhard rod, hardware we purchased from Speedway Motors,” shares Fogarty. Also from Speedway are coil-over rear dampers and a solid front axle equipped with leaf springs.


Fogarty and Hale removed the body from the frame and mounted it on my rotisserie to strip the entire floor pan. They replaced it with four fresh pieces obtained from the National Chevy Association—two toe panels, a firewall providing room for the larger engine, and a trunk floor supporting a new 16-gallon fuel tank.


Courtesy Ron Fogarty


Courtesy Ron Fogarty


Courtesy Ron Fogarty


Fogarty had the stock bench seat reupholstered nearby at a shop called Car City Complete. Since the Chevy was born a Business Coupe, it had no rear seat and a long trunk to accommodate bulky sales materials.


“My most notable contributions—beyond paying the bills—were a fresh paint job and new wiring throughout the car,” says Fogarty. “The Toyota Renaissance Red paint I sprayed was topped with a matte clear coat for a weathered appearance. To complete the patina, I sprayed black-matte paint onto a rag, which I rubbed here and there around the exterior.”


(L-R) Car owner Ron Fogarty; Mike Hale who performed the welding of fabricated parts and both the bodywork and painting with Fogarty; John Martin who built the car’s engine; and Tim Egan who rounded up parts and trailered the finish product to car shows.


Don Sherman


The new springs lift the car high enough to provide ample clearance in the back for Mickey Thompson P295/65R-15 ET Street S/S radials. The front tires, Mickey Thompson Sportsman 29×7.5-15LT tires mounted to American Racing aluminum wheels, are *not* radials. “My suspicion is that this contributes to my car’s tendency to wander when the driver wishes to head straight,” says Fogarty.


Also on the fresh parts list are a large aluminum radiator from Champion Radiators and Wilwood vented disc front brakes. Speedway Motors supplied the new dual master cylinder and vacuum booster and a steering column that twists a Chevy Vega steering gear.


Courtesy Ron Fogarty


“Start to finish, my Chevy Gas Coupe required six years of effort and $10,000 for the car, plus $5000 for the engine. The lion’s share of the new components came from aftermarket parts catalogues. Since Grampas Toy—a nod to my three grandchildren and six great-grandchildren—became roadworthy seven years ago, I’ve driven it about 1500 miles, primarily to car shows,” says Fogarty.


Proving that his ingenuity is exceeded only by his generosity, Mr. Fogarty granted our request to drive his Pride and Toy. Challenge *numero uno:* climbing aboard. With the ride height knocking on heaven’s gate (for improved weight transfer and traction at the strip), athleticism is essential to mount the driver’s seat. Sliding that bench forward to reach the wood-rimmed steering wheel is also difficult. Thankfully, lap belts have been added to this period piece to help restrain occupants in the event of an abrupt stop.


Turn the key, and the music broadcast through the headers and mini mufflers is both the best bass refrain ever orchestrated and just quiet enough to slip past enforcement fellows. The B&M floor shifter has a convenient automatic mode for road use, which we selected to start our 10-mile journey about Mr. Fogarty’s neighborhood.


In every respect, Fogarty’s Chevy is a trip back in time. The high-effort, unassisted steering offers major slack when you least need it. While the acceleration doesn’t threaten a current Corvette, it’s strong enough to let traffic know there’s a belligerent kid in town. The grand AutoMeter tachometer strapped to the steering column hustles toward 5000 rpm every time you stomp the right pedal. Shifting is so automatic it can’t be felt. Ride motions are, for all intents, unpredictable. The best news is the brakes: they are powerful, predictable, and easily controlled by the round pedal jutting proudly from the floor.


Bottom line: Grampas Toy achieves its gasser goal in use and execution. It’s clear why Fogarty enjoys driving his creation now and then to collect a fresh sparkler for his trophy case.
